summary_plain: This investigation used computer simulations to study how smoke forms and grows when materials heat up and release vapors without flames. By comparing conditions on Earth to microgravity, researchers examined how the lack of buoyancy alters particle movement and smoke composition. Understanding these smoke characteristics is crucial for designing better smoke detectors to keep astronauts safe in space.
summary_expert: The investigation utilized direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach to examine the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. The study evaluated two inlet velocities (Uo = 0.08 m/s and Uo = 0.1 m/s), two geometric configurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. Results showed that in Earth gravity, buoyancy produces asymmetries and gravitational settling removes large particles, limiting maximum particle size to approximately 40 micrometers and mode size to approximately 5 micrometers. In microgravity, the smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles greater than 40 micrometers, with a bimodal distribution appearing when prominent high-temperature recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source.

key_findings.text: Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol in Earth gravity, limiting the maximum particle size to approximately 40 micrometers and the mode particle size to approximately 5 micrometers.
Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles greater than 40 micrometers.
In microgravity without recirculation, the mode particle diameter is approximately 10 micrometers, which is approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke.

The peak number density in Case 1MG-NT (no thermophoresis) is greater than Case 1MG by approximately a factor of five, with the most frequent particle size being approximately 5 micrometers for both cases.
